summary: This sample is the Fe-35Mn-19Al-5Cu (at.%) low-density steel — designated "19Al" according to its Al content — in the state obtained by solution treatment at 1100 °C for 10 min (oil quenched) followed by aging at 600 °C for 1 h and water quenching. It belongs to a study of how Al content (15, 17, 19 at.%) controls the aging-hardening behaviour of Fe-Mn-Al-Cu low-density steels, in which the ultra-hard β-Mn phase precipitates continuously during aging. After only 1 h at 600 °C the α (BCC) matrix had almost completely transformed into β-Mn, giving a Vickers hardness of 901.2 ± 14.6 HV, one of the near-peak values of the 19Al alloy.
composition: Nominal composition Fe-35Mn-19Al-5Cu (at.%), produced from high-purity (>99.9 %) raw materials. EDS-measured composition (Table 1): Fe 41.6, Mn 34.8, Al 18.6, Cu 5.0 at.%. Al is the principal density-reducing element (about 0.1 g·cm⁻³ density reduction per 1 wt.% Al) and, being an Al-rich BCC/D0₃ stabilizer, also influences β-Mn precipitation and solid-solution strengthening; the high 35 at.% Mn level was chosen to promote the precipitation kinetics of the hard β-Mn phase; Cu was added to accelerate aging hardening and raise hardness (building on the authors' earlier Fe-Mn-Al-Cu alloy). The measured Archimedes density of the 19Al alloy is 6.66 g·cm⁻³ (the lowest of the three alloys: 6.85 for 15Al, 6.76 for 17Al).
processing: Ingots were melted in a vacuum induction furnace under an argon atmosphere. The ingots were homogenized at 1200 °C for 24 h and then hot-rolled into plates 4 mm thick. The plates were cut by electrical discharge machining into 10 × 5 × 2 mm³ samples for hardness measurement and microstructural characterization. Samples were solution treated at 1100 °C for 10 min under an argon atmosphere, followed by oil quenching (the parent process, proc_st-1100c-10min-oq), which yields a single-phase α (BCC) matrix. The solution-treated 19Al samples were then aged at 600 °C for 1 h (within the study's overall aging window of 525–650 °C for 1, 3, 6 and 10 h), followed by water quenching. Surfaces for hardness, XRD, SEM and EBSD were prepared by electrolytic polishing in 10 % perchloric acid + 90 % ethanol.
microstructure: After aging at 600 °C for 1 h the α (BCC) matrix of the 19Al alloy had almost completely transformed into β-Mn, leaving a predominantly β-Mn structure in which numerous fine precipitates are distributed within the β-Mn and at the β-Mn interfaces. Four phases are resolved: the dominant β-Mn matrix (formed by the near-complete α→β-Mn transformation), residual α (BCC), a newly formed fine BCC phase distributed within the β-Mn, and a fine FCC Cu-rich phase located at the interfaces between β-Mn grains. In this condition the transformation has therefore reached the final stage of the proposed Fe-Mn-Al-Cu aging sequence α → α + FCC Cu-rich phase → α-Mn + β-Mn + BCC phase → β-Mn + BCC phase + FCC Cu-rich phase. SE-SEM of the same 600 °C/1 h condition shows a β-Mn matrix with fine secondary features, consistent with the near-complete α→β-Mn transformation (Fig. 9). Across the alloy series the FCC Cu-rich phase content between β-Mn interfaces decreases with increasing Al content, while the total amount of BCC and FCC Cu-rich precipitates at the β-Mn interfaces grows with Al content (reaching 6.5 % for 19Al aged at 650 °C for 6 h, versus 3.9 % for 15Al at 650 °C/3 h and 4.7 % for 17Al at 650 °C/10 h). The solution-treated starting state (1100 °C/10 min + OQ) is a single α (BCC) phase whose grain structure is markedly refined as Al increases from 15 to 19 at.%.
properties: Vickers hardness (HVS-1000 digital microhardness tester, 9.8 N for 15 s, five measurements averaged on electrolytically polished 10 × 5 × 2 mm³ samples): 901.2 ± 14.6 HV for this 19Al 600 °C/1 h condition — one of the near-peak values of the 19Al alloy (Table 4). At 600 °C the 19Al hardness is uniformly high and nearly time-independent (901.2 ± 14.6, 899.8 ± 6.8, 895.3 ± 16.2 and 917.8 ± 24.5 HV at 1, 3, 6 and 10 h), so temperature rather than time governs the hardness level, and the alloy's overall aged hardness window spans 263.8 HV (solution-treated baseline) to 917.8 HV. Density: 6.66 g·cm⁻³ (Archimedes). For context on the same alloy family, the ultra-hard 19Al condition (600 °C/10 h, 917.8 HV) had a β-Mn intrinsic hardness of 12.5 ± 0.4 GPa by nanoindentation and a fracture toughness K_IC of 3.5 MPa·m^1/2, both part of the general trend that increasing Al raises β-Mn intrinsic hardness but lowers alloy toughness. Characterization applied to this material in the study comprises Vickers microhardness testing, secondary-electron SEM (ZEISS Sigma 300, 5 kV), XRD (D8 Discover), EBSD (GeminiSEM 300) and TEM (FEI Talos F200X, 200 kV) plus nanoindentation (Agilent G200, 200 nm depth) on the hardest states.
mechanisms: α→β-Mn transformation as the hardening mechanism: aging produces a continuous precipitation of the ultra-hard β-Mn phase; at 600 °C and above the α matrix of the 19Al alloy transforms almost completely into β-Mn within only 1 h, and because β-Mn has an intrinsic hardness above 10 GPa (12.5 ± 0.4 GPa for the hardest 19Al state), the extensive formation of β-Mn is what raises the alloy to ultra-high hardness (901.2 ± 14.6 HV here).

Temperature accelerates β-Mn precipitation: the increase of aging temperature raises both the driving force for β-Mn formation and the atomic diffusion rate, which is why the α→β-Mn transformation of the 19Al alloy required only 1 h at 600 °C, whereas at 525 °C only 12.1 % β-Mn formed even after 10 h and at 550 °C the transformation needed 10 h.

Al slows β-Mn precipitation kinetics (diffusion/redistribution argument): β-Mn is a Mn-rich phase whose nucleation and growth must expel large amounts of other atoms (it is rich in Mn but poor in Al and Cu). A higher Al content means more Al atoms enriched around β-Mn, which hinders its further precipitation and growth, so the 19Al alloy transforms more slowly than 15Al and 17Al.

Al slows β-Mn precipitation kinetics (D0₃ argument): Al strongly stabilizes the Al-rich D0₃ phase, so higher Al content increases the amount and size of D0₃ and stabilizes it; because β-Mn nucleation and growth require the prior depletion of D0₃, this retards the β-Mn transformation. Consistently, D0₃ is absent in the maximum-hardness states where β-Mn has grown.

New BCC phase formation at β-Mn interfaces: as β-Mn grows it expels Fe, Al and Cu into the surrounding matrix; the resulting enrichment of Al (a BCC-stabilizing element) around the β-Mn interfaces produces the fine BCC precipitates observed within/at the β-Mn interfaces.

FCC Cu-rich phase formation at β-Mn interfaces: Cu is expelled from β-Mn during its precipitation and growth and has limited solubility in Fe-based alloys, so fine FCC Cu-rich particles (frequently containing FCC twins, verified by SAED and EDS mapping showing Cu enrichment with Fe and Mn depletion) form at the β-Mn interfaces.

Hardness controlled by both intrinsic β-Mn hardness and the β-Mn volume fraction: increasing Al slightly raises the intrinsic hardness of β-Mn (Al dissolved in β-Mn rises from 14.3 at.% in 15Al to 16.3 at.% in 17Al and 17.5 at.% in 19Al, i.e. solid-solution strengthening), but it simultaneously increases the content of the softer FCC Cu-rich and BCC precipitates at β-Mn interfaces, lowering the absolute volume fraction of β-Mn and therefore the overall hardness — explaining why the peak hardness of the alloy family decreases with increasing Al content.

Toughness–hardness trade-off with Al: higher Al raises β-Mn intrinsic hardness (which should degrade K_IC) and reduces the amount of the relatively ductile FCC Cu-rich phase at the β-Mn interfaces, so K_IC of the ultra-hard Fe-Mn-Al-Cu steels decreases with increasing Al content (8.6 MPa·m^1/2 for 15Al, 6.6 for 17Al and 3.5 for 19Al at their peak-hardness states).
conclusions: The 19Al alloy aged at 600 °C for 1 h is a near-peak-hardness state of the highest-Al member of the Fe-35Mn-(15,17,19)Al-5Cu series: the α (BCC) matrix has almost completely transformed into ultra-hard β-Mn within just 1 h, yielding 901.2 ± 14.6 HV, and the 19Al hardness at 600 °C is essentially flat between 1 and 10 h (peak 917.8 ± 24.5 HV at 600 °C/10 h). The ultra-wide, flexible hardness window of these Fe-Mn-Al-Cu low-density steels (253.4–965.6 HV over the whole series; 263.8–917.8 HV for 19Al) means parts can be shaped in the soft solution-treated state and then aged to a chosen hardness, saving fabrication time and cost. Increasing Al content raises density reduction (6.66 g·cm⁻³ for 19Al) and the intrinsic hardness of β-Mn, but it also slows the β-Mn precipitation kinetics, shifts the optimal ultra-high-hardness aging window to higher temperature (about 575–625 °C for 19Al versus 525–600 °C for 15Al) and lowers fracture toughness, so density reduction must be balanced against mechanical performance. The alloys achieve specific hardness above 140 HV·cm³/g (141 HV·cm³/g for the 15Al alloy), the highest among low-density steels, other steels, pure iron and medium/high-entropy alloys considered in the study, though the toughness of the ultra-hard states still needs improvement.
unmapped: This 19Al 600 °C/1 h sample is distinct from the 19Al peak-hardness condition of the paper, which is 600 °C for 10 h (917.8 ± 24.5 HV); the solution-treated 19Al baseline is 263.8 ± 1.1 HV.

The optimal aging temperature window for ultra-high hardness shifts upward with Al content: about 525–600 °C for 15Al, 550–600 °C for 17Al and 575–625 °C for 19Al (from the hardness contour maps, Fig. 2).

Al content also refines the solution-treated grain structure: the 19Al alloy shows a much finer equiaxed grain structure than 15Al or 17Al, while all three solution-treated alloys are single-phase α (BCC).
